analysis.one_liner: Lets children under 16 sue social media companies for bodily injury or mental-health harm.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new federal lawsuit right for anyone who, as a child under 16, suffered bodily injury or mental-health harm partly attributable to using a social media platform. A family could sue the company in federal or state court for actual damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees — and even without proving specific dollar losses, could claim a minimum amount equal to a per-user slice of the company's U.S. revenue for every year the child was harmed. Companies could escape liability only by showing they verified every user's age and had no reason to know the user was under 16.
analysis.who_benefits: Children who were harmed by social media use and their families, who would gain a powerful new legal claim that is easier to win than ordinary negligence suits, with guaranteed minimum payouts and fee-shifting that makes lawyers willing to take the cases.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal private right of action allowing a person harmed as a minor to sue a social media company for bodily injury or mental-health harm attributable, in whole or in part, to use of the platform.

Sets a guaranteed minimum compensatory damages floor: for each year of harm, the company's U.S. annual revenue divided by its fewest monthly active users that year, summed across years — in addition to actual damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees and costs.
Allows suits in federal district court or any state court of competent jurisdiction, and takes effect 180 days after enactment, applying only to use after that date.

analysis.who_pays: Social media companies, which would face potentially enormous per-user revenue-based damages, punitive awards, and litigation costs — and might respond by restricting minors' access or building age-verification systems.

drawbacks.text: The causation standard is very low: a plaintiff need only show harm 'attributable, in whole or in part' to platform use, and the bill requires no showing that the company did anything wrong — liability attaches to the use itself, absent an affirmative defense.

The damages formula assigns each harmed child a per-user share of the company's entire U.S. annual revenue for every year of alleged harm, on top of punitive damages, which could produce awards vastly out of proportion to any proven injury and drive broad shutdowns or restrictions of services used by minors.

The only safe harbor is proving the company verified the age of every user at all relevant times, which pushes platforms toward age verification for all users — raising privacy concerns — or toward banning minors outright.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targets is real: platforms profit from engagement-heavy products used heavily by minors, and ordinary negligence law has struggled to hold them accountable. But the remedy is blunt. Near-automatic liability, a revenue-based minimum damages formula, and punitive awards stacked on top would expose platforms to staggering sums for any harm 'in part' connected to use — a design that courts would likely struggle with and that would push companies to exclude young users rather than make products safer. A narrower standard tied to specific platform conduct would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the bill on September 30, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media companies, which avoided any exposure to the new child-injury liability, and no one else — the bill produced no protections because it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Social media platforms avoided new liability

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; it was his proposal alone.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Richard Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: 0 of 99 other senators
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors over the bill's 27 months of existence.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded; the sole sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have made platforms strictly liable for injuries or mental-health harm to under-16 users, with a revenue-based minimum damages formula per harmed child plus punitive damages — potentially enormous aggregate exposure. Platforms' interest in avoiding this liability runs against the families seeking recourse, though the platforms' likely response (age-gating or excluding minors) would also affect young users.

industries.industry: Advertising-supported internet services and apps with social features
industries.note: The bill's definition covers any interactive computer service with accounts and third-party content sharing that is not mainly peer-to-peer messaging, reaching far beyond the largest platforms to smaller apps, forums, and services. Those businesses would face the same liability design without the largest firms' legal resources.
